context.guidance: Protect each Tier A and Tier B Personal Data Element at field or column level before it is stored, with keys held outside the data store, so that a database dump or a restored backup does not reveal the values. Disk or volume encryption protects only the storage medium, so it lowers severity without clearing the Finding. Until DPDP §44(2) omits IT Act §43A, that section's reasonable-security duty applies alongside Rule 6(1)(a).

value.fix: Stop storing the card number as a plain INTEGER column. Encrypt it at the field level in the application before it reaches the database, with the encryption key held outside the data store (for example in a KMS or HSM, not in the database or the same config as the data). Change the column type to TEXT or BYTEA to hold the ciphertext, and apply the existing 16-digit numeric check to the plaintext before encryption. Sequelize getters and setters can handle the encrypt and decrypt steps. If the card number is needed only for lookup or matching, store a keyed HMAC (blind index) alongside it instead of the raw value. Where possible, avoid storing the full PAN at all by tokenizing it with the payment gateway or keeping only the last four digits. Disk or volume encryption alone does not clear this finding, because a database dump or restored backup would still expose the plaintext values. Note that the current INTEGER type cannot hold the stated maximum of 9999999999999998 on most SQL databases (PostgreSQL INTEGER tops out at 2147483647), so the column is already misdefined and must change in the same migration.
